finding.claim: iconUrl is stored without any validation and later fetched by the nightly job with an HTTP GET, which gives SSRF. An authenticated user can set it to internal hosts, cloud metadata (http://169.254.169.254/...), or localhost services. The webhookUrl field is SAFE: String.matches is a full-match check against a fixed host and a 20-character alphanumeric path.
finding.source: icon parameter of PUT /profile -> Profile.update(webhook, icon)
finding.sink: HttpClient.send(HttpRequest GET to URI.create(iconUrl)) in Profile.sync

trace.note: update(webhook, icon): icon is attacker-controlled input from PUT /profile
this.iconUrl = icon is stored with no scheme, host or IP validation (second-order flow)
nightly job sync(HttpClient c) runs later
URI.create(iconUrl) is requested with GET and the response body is read as bytes

finding.guards_checked: The only check in update() is the regex on webhook (line 12). It is never applied to icon. There is no allowlist, no private-IP or metadata-address blocking, and no scheme check. The HttpClient is passed in and its configuration is not visible; the default client does not follow redirects, which does not mitigate direct access to internal URLs.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores `icon` unvalidated (the only check, at line 12, covers `webhook` only) and src/Profile.java:23 issues a GET to URI.create(iconUrl), so an authenticated user can aim it at internal hosts.
